curricula.title: Angular
curricula.summary: For someone who knows TypeScript and needs the framework's model rather than its vocabulary. About dependency injection, change detection and reactive data flow.

activities.title: The view that stops updating
activities.prompt: A component with OnPush shows stale data after its input object is modified in place. Why?
activities.explanation: OnPush trades "check everything constantly" for "check when something observably changed", and reference identity is how it observes. Replace the object rather than mutating it and the view updates. This is the same discipline immutable state buys elsewhere, and it is why OnPush and mutation are a bad pairing.

options.text: OnPush re-checks when an input reference changes, and mutating the object does not change it.
OnPush disables change detection entirely for that component.
options.why: It still runs on events, async pipe emissions and reference changes. It narrows when, not whether.

options.text: The component needs to be declared in a different module.
options.why: Module declaration has no bearing on change detection strategy.

options.text: OnPush requires zone.js to be disabled.
options.why: They are independent, and OnPush is the more useful of the two either way.

activities.title: The subscription that outlives the component
activities.prompt: This leaks every time the component is destroyed and recreated. Which line?
activities.explanation: Nothing unsubscribes, so the callback survives the component and keeps a reference to it — the component is never collected and its handler keeps running against a dead view. Either let the template subscribe with the async pipe, which unsubscribes for you, or tie the subscription to the component's lifetime explicitly.

activities.title: Where a provider lives
activities.prompt: Match each provider declaration to how many instances exist.
activities.explanation: Scope is a lifetime decision, not a wiring detail. A service holding per-component state provided in root becomes shared state between components that were meant to be independent, which presents as one widget changing when you interact with another.

pairs.right: One per instance of that component
One shared across applications on the page

activities.title: switchMap against mergeMap
activities.prompt: A search box emits "a" then "ab" quickly. The request for "a" is slower than the one for "ab". With switchMap, which result reaches the view?
activities.explanation: `switchMap` cancels the previous inner observable when a new value arrives, so the request for "a" is unsubscribed and its late response is discarded. With `mergeMap` both would be live and the slower "a" would arrive last and overwrite the view — the out-of-order search result bug, which is why switchMap is the right default for typeahead.

activities.title: When the input actually arrives
activities.prompt: A child logs in its constructor and in ngOnInit. What prints?
activities.explanation: Inputs are set by the framework *after* construction and *before* ngOnInit — that window is the whole reason ngOnInit exists. Code in the constructor sees the field initializer, not the binding, which is why initialization that depends on an input belongs in ngOnInit and why a constructor in Angular should mostly just receive dependencies.

activities.title: Two components, two services, one surprise
activities.prompt: A service is in `providers` of two component decorators. Both components inject it and see different data. Why?
activities.explanation: Where a provider is registered decides how many instances exist. `providedIn: 'root'` means one for the application; a `providers` entry on a component means one per component instance, created with it and destroyed with it. Both are useful — per-component state wants the narrow one — but mixing them up produces exactly this bug: two islands of state where one shared service was intended.

options.text: A component-level provider creates one instance per component; each component got its own.
Angular services are never shared; every injection is a new instance.
options.why: A service provided in root is one instance for the whole application. Sharing is the default people rely on.

options.text: The service must be marked @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) to work at all.
options.why: providedIn root is one way to register, not a requirement. Component providers are legal and sometimes exactly right.

options.text: One of the injections silently failed and returned a mock.
options.why: A failed injection throws at construction. Angular does not invent fallbacks.

activities.title: A derived value that stays derived
activities.prompt: Complete this so the total always reflects the items, with no subscription.
activities.explanation: `computed` re-evaluates when the signals it read change, and only then. The alternative — storing the total and updating it wherever items change — is the two-sources-of-truth bug waiting for the one code path that forgets. A derived value should be written as a derivation, and signals make that the cheap option as well as the correct one.
activities.template:
items = signal<Item[]>([]);
total = {1}(() => this.items().reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0));

blanks.hint: The signal that is a function of other signals.

activities.title: Which mechanism carries what
activities.prompt: Match each need to the mechanism that serves it.
activities.explanation: The first two are the everyday pair, and their direction is the point: data flows down through inputs, events flow up through outputs, and nothing reaches sideways. Projection is for when the parent owns the *content*, not just the data — a card component that renders whatever you put between its tags. When several distant components need the same state, threading inputs through every layer is the smell; a service is the shared place.

pairs.left: Parent supplies markup to render inside
Many components share one growing state

curricula.title: Architecture
curricula.summary: Architecture as programming, not as diagrams. Every exercise is a codebase with a measurable defect — an import cycle, a second source of truth, an operation that is not safe to retry — and you fix it until the property holds. The tests assert the property, not the drawing.

skills.name: Changing a decision you already shipped
The cost of a solution nobody needed

activities.title: The cycle
activities.prompt: `orders` imports from `billing`, and `billing` imports from `orders`. Which statement about this is a fact rather than an opinion?
activities.explanation: A cycle is a checkable property of the import graph, and its consequence is mechanical: you cannot load, test or reason about either module in isolation, and a change to one can reach itself through the other. What to do about it is a design decision. That it exists is not.

options.text: Neither module can be built, tested or understood without the other.
It will be slower at runtime.
options.why: A cycle in the module graph has no inherent runtime cost. The cost is entirely to change and comprehension.

options.text: It means the two should be merged.
options.why: Sometimes true and sometimes the opposite. That is the judgment call; the question asks for the fact.

options.text: It will fail to compile in most languages.
options.why: Most languages permit it. The tooling not stopping you is why cycles accumulate.

activities.title: Breaking a cycle with an interface
activities.prompt: Order these steps to remove the orders/billing cycle by dependency inversion.
activities.explanation: The interface is declared by the consumer, which is what actually reverses the arrow: `billing` now depends on `orders`, and `orders` depends on nothing. Declaring it in a shared module instead leaves both depending on the shared one and is a common way to do this and get no benefit.
lines: Identify what orders actually needs from billing: one call, charge()
Declare a PaymentGateway interface inside orders
Change orders to depend on PaymentGateway, not on billing
Wire the concrete billing implementation at the composition root
Delete the import of billing from orders

activities.title: Which decision to spend time on
activities.prompt: Two decisions are on the table. Which deserves the longer discussion?
activities.explanation: Sort decisions by how hard they are to undo, not by how interesting they are. A published API shape is depended on by people you cannot deploy alongside, so changing it needs versioning, migration and coordination — it is close to irreversible. Spend your deliberation budget there and decide the reversible things fast.

options.text: The public shape of an API other teams will build against.
Which logging library to use inside one service.
options.why: Reversible in an afternoon by one person. Deciding it quickly and badly costs almost nothing.

options.text: The name of an internal module.
options.why: A rename is a mechanical refactor with tool support.

options.text: Which of two equivalent JSON parsers to depend on.
options.why: Swappable behind the same call. If it were not swappable, that would be the actual problem.

activities.title: Two sources of truth
activities.prompt: This will eventually report a total that disagrees with the rows. Which line introduces that?
activities.explanation: The total is a second copy of a fact the rows already contain, written by a separate statement that can fail on its own. Anything derivable should be derived; if it must be stored for performance, it has to be written in the same transaction as the thing it summarizes, so the two cannot disagree.
activities.correction: derive the total when reading, or update it in the same transaction as the insert

activities.title: Replacing a system that is in use
activities.prompt: A ten-year-old service must be replaced. It cannot stop working during the process. What does the strangler approach actually require first?
activities.explanation: The facade is what makes incremental replacement possible: with it, one operation at a time can be routed to the new implementation, compared against the old, and rolled back on its own. Without it there is no unit of migration smaller than the whole system, and no way to undo a slice that goes wrong.

options.text: A facade in front of the old system, so traffic can be routed per operation.
A complete rewrite on a branch, cut over when finished.
options.why: This is the big-bang rewrite the pattern exists to avoid — the branch diverges, the cutover is one enormous untested event, and there is no way back.

options.text: Freezing changes to the old system until the new one is ready.
options.why: A freeze means the business stops while you work, which is usually not on offer and grows the gap between the two systems.

options.text: Full test coverage of the old system before starting.
options.why: Desirable, often impossible, and not the first step. Characterization tests come per-slice, as each is moved.

curricula.title: ASP.NET
curricula.summary: For someone building services on .NET who wants the pipeline rather than the scaffolding. About middleware, model binding, and the parts of a request that fail under load.

activities.title: The captive dependency
activities.prompt: A singleton service takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor. What happens?
activities.explanation: This is a captive dependency: the shorter lifetime is trapped inside the longer one. The context is never disposed, its change tracker grows all day, and concurrent requests share one non-thread-safe object. Inject `IServiceScopeFactory` and create a scope per unit of work instead.

options.text: The context is captured for the lifetime of the application, outliving every request scope it was meant to serve.
A new context is resolved per request automatically.
options.why: Constructor injection resolves once, when the singleton is built. Nothing re-resolves it later.

options.text: It is fine, because DbContext is thread-safe.
options.why: It is explicitly not thread-safe, which makes this worse rather than better.

options.text: The container refuses to start.
options.why: Validation catches this only when scope validation is enabled — on by default in Development, and often not in Production.

activities.title: Pipeline order
activities.prompt: Put these into the order that actually works.
activities.explanation: Order is behavior here, not style. Exception handling must be outermost to catch everything inside it. Routing has to run before authorization, because the endpoint is what carries the policy. Authentication must precede authorization — you cannot check permissions for a user you have not identified yet. Getting the last two the wrong way round produces endpoints that are silently unprotected.

activities.title: A read that gets slower all day
activities.prompt: A read-only endpoint loading thousands of rows uses more memory and time than expected. What is the one-line improvement?
activities.explanation: By default EF Core keeps a snapshot of every entity it materializes so it can detect changes on save. For a query that will never be saved, that is double the memory and a fixup pass for nothing. `AsNoTracking` skips it, and for read endpoints it is close to free.

options.text: Add AsNoTracking to the query.
Add an index.
options.why: Worth doing, and a different problem. The symptom here is on the client side of the query.

options.text: Increase the connection pool.
options.why: The connection is not the constraint; the materialized objects are.

options.text: Use a stored procedure.
options.why: Moves the query, keeps the tracking. The entities are still tracked when they come back.

activities.title: Status codes
activities.prompt: Match each situation to the status it should return.
activities.explanation: 401 and 403 are the pair that gets confused: 401 means "I do not know who you are, try authenticating", 403 means "I know exactly who you are and the answer is no". Returning 401 for a permissions failure sends clients into a login loop that cannot succeed.

pairs.left: Credentials were fine, permission was not
The route matched but the id does not exist

activities.title: The cached user that belongs to someone else
activities.prompt: A singleton service holds a `CurrentUser` property set from the request. In production, users intermittently see someone else's name. Why?
activities.explanation: Singleton means one instance for the application; scoped means one per request; transient means one per injection. Per-request state in a singleton is therefore shared mutable state under concurrency — the symptom is intermittent, the report is unreproducible, and the fix is almost always to make the service scoped or to stop storing the state. The related trap is captive dependency: injecting a scoped service into a singleton quietly extends its life to the application's.

options.text: A singleton is one instance for every request at once; concurrent requests overwrite each other's user.
The property needs to be marked volatile.
options.why: Memory visibility is not the problem. The design shares one slot between requests; no keyword fixes that.

options.text: The load balancer is routing users to the wrong server.
options.why: Then everything about the session would be wrong, not one property, and it would not correlate with concurrency.

options.text: Scoped services are slower, so ASP.NET promoted it to singleton.
options.why: Lifetimes never change on their own. The registration says singleton because someone wrote singleton.

activities.title: Where the argument actually came from
activities.prompt: `GET /products/7?page=2` reaches `Get(int id, int page, [FromHeader] string accept)`. Where does each argument come from?
activities.explanation: Simple types bind route-first, then query string — which is why `id` matches the `{id}` template segment and `page` falls through to the query. Headers and bodies are never guessed; they take an explicit [FromHeader] or [FromBody]. The rule worth keeping: binding is convention until the convention is ambiguous, and then the attribute is documentation as much as configuration.

options.text: id from the route, page from the query string, accept from the Accept header.
All three from the query string.
options.why: id appears in the route template, and binding checks the route before the query.

options.text: The body, because GET requests bind from the body by default.
options.why: A GET has no body worth speaking of, and binding from one requires [FromBody] explicitly.

options.text: It fails to compile without [FromQuery] on everything.
options.why: Attributes override the defaults; they are not required for them.

activities.title: Configuration with a type and a check
activities.prompt: Complete this so the settings bind from configuration and a missing api key fails at startup rather than on the first request.
activities.explanation: The options pattern gives configuration a type, and types can be validated. The default timing is the trap: validation runs when the options are first resolved, which is the first request that needs them — the worst possible moment to learn a key is missing. ValidateOnStart moves the failure to boot, where a bad deploy is caught by the deploy rather than by a customer.
activities.template:
builder.Services.AddOptions<MailSettings>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Mail"))
    .Validate(settings => !string.IsNullOrEmpty(settings.ApiKey), "Mail:ApiKey is required")
    .{1}();

blanks.hint: Without it, validation runs lazily — on the first resolve, mid-request.

activities.title: Liveness is not readiness
activities.prompt: Complete the readiness endpoint so the orchestrator stops sending traffic while the database is unreachable, without restarting the process.
activities.explanation: Liveness answers "should this process be restarted" and must not depend on the database — a dead dependency would put every instance into a restart loop that fixes nothing. Readiness answers "should this instance receive traffic", and that is exactly where dependency checks belong: the instance waits out the outage and rejoins when the check passes.

blanks.hint: The probe that gates traffic rather than survival.

curricula.title: Backend
curricula.summary: Language-agnostic service work: designing an interface, storing things, and failing without losing data. About the properties that only appear under concurrency and load.

skills.name: Errors a caller can act on
At least once, and what that forces

activities.title: The double charge
activities.prompt: A payment request times out. The client retries and the customer is charged twice. What fixes this properly?
activities.explanation: A timeout tells you nothing about whether the server did the work. The only sound answer is to make the operation idempotent: the client supplies a key, the server stores the outcome against it, and every repeat of that key returns the stored outcome instead of doing the work again. The key must come from the client, because only the client knows that two requests are the same intent.

options.text: Stop retrying on timeout.
options.why: Then a request lost in transit silently fails. Retries are correct; unsafe retries are the problem.

options.text: The client sends a key with the request, and the server records it and returns the first result on any repeat.
Make the client wait longer before retrying.
options.why: This changes how often the race happens, not whether it can. A timeout never tells you the work did not happen.

options.text: Check for a recent identical charge before creating one.
options.why: Closer, but "identical" is a guess, and two genuine purchases of the same thing are indistinguishable from a retry.

activities.title: The service that stops responding
activities.prompt: A dependency slows to 30 seconds per call. Your service, which has no client timeout, stops serving *all* traffic. Why?
activities.explanation: This is resource exhaustion, and it is how one slow dependency takes down a service that does ten other things. A timeout shorter than your own response budget bounds the damage; a circuit breaker stops sending traffic to something already known to be failing. Every remote call needs a timeout, and the default in most clients is no timeout at all.

options.text: Every worker ends up blocked waiting on the slow dependency, so nothing is left to serve anything else.
The dependency is returning errors that propagate.
options.why: It is returning correct responses, only slowly. Nothing has errored yet, which is what makes this hard to spot.

options.text: The operating system throttles the process for having open sockets.
options.why: No such mechanism. The exhaustion is of your own worker pool.

options.text: Memory fills with queued responses.
options.why: Memory may well rise, but the outage is caused by workers being unavailable, not by allocation.

activities.title: Lost update
activities.prompt: Two requests decrement stock at the same time and the count ends up one too high. Which line makes that possible?
activities.explanation: The value read on line 1 is stale by the time it is written on line 3, so two concurrent requests both read 5 and both write 4. Doing the arithmetic in the database makes it atomic, and putting the condition in the WHERE clause makes the check atomic with it. Read-modify-write across a network round trip is a race unless something guards it.
activities.correction: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0

activities.title: Paging a moving list
activities.prompt: Users report that items are occasionally skipped while paging through a feed that receives new entries. The API uses OFFSET and LIMIT. Why?
activities.explanation: Offset paging assumes the list holds still. Cursor paging asks for "everything after this key" instead, which is stable under insertion and also avoids the database counting past a million rows to reach page twenty thousand. Offsets are fine for a static report and wrong for a feed.

options.text: An insert before the current offset shifts everything, so the next page starts past an unseen row.
OFFSET is capped by the database.
options.why: Large offsets are slow but not silently truncated; the symptom would be latency, not gaps.

options.text: The client is caching pages.
options.why: A cache would repeat rows, not skip them.

options.text: LIMIT and OFFSET cannot be combined with ORDER BY.
options.why: They routinely are, and must be — without an ORDER BY the paging is meaningless.

activities.title: Latency numbers
activities.prompt: Match each measure to what it actually tells you.
activities.explanation: Averages are the wrong summary for latency because the distribution is not symmetric — a handful of ten-second requests barely move the mean and are the entire user complaint. p99 matters more than it sounds: a user making a hundred requests to load one page hits it about once every page.

pairs.right: Hides the slow tail almost completely
The experience of your busiest users
One event, often a deploy or a cold start

curricula.title: C
curricula.summary: For someone who wants to know what the machine is actually doing. About memory you manage yourself, and the discipline that makes that survivable.

skills.name: Arrays, and the decay to a pointer
malloc, free, and ownership by convention

activities.title: Returning what is gone
activities.prompt: This function sometimes works and sometimes prints rubbish. Which line is the fault?
activities.explanation: `buffer` lives on the stack and its lifetime ends when the function returns, so the caller receives a pointer to memory that has been handed back. It often still holds the right bytes, which is what makes this bug survive testing. Either allocate it, take a caller-supplied buffer, or return a string literal.
activities.correction: char *buffer = malloc(32);  /* and the caller frees it */

activities.title: sizeof, and where it stops working
activities.prompt: On a 64-bit machine, what does this print?
activities.explanation: An array knows its own size only where it is declared. Passed to a function it decays to a pointer, so `sizeof` reports the pointer size, not the array. This is why every C function taking an array also takes a length — there is no way to recover it.

activities.title: Room for the terminator
activities.prompt: How much memory does a copy of the string "hello" need?
activities.explanation: A C string is the characters followed by a NUL byte, and every function that reads one relies on that byte to know where to stop. `strlen` returns 5 and `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)` is the idiom for exactly this reason. The missing `+ 1` is one of the most common heap overflows in the language.

options.text: 5 bytes, one per character.
options.why: This is the mistake that writes a NUL byte one past the end of the allocation.

options.text: 6 bytes, the characters plus a terminating NUL.
8 bytes, rounded up for alignment.
options.why: The allocator may round up internally; what you must ask for is what you will write.

options.text: Whatever `sizeof("hello")` reports at the call site, which is 5.
options.why: `sizeof` on a string literal is 6 — it includes the terminator. That is the point of the question.

activities.title: One exit path
activities.prompt: Put this into the order that releases everything exactly once on every path.
activities.explanation: The labels unwind in the reverse order of acquisition, and each failure jumps to the point that releases everything acquired so far. This is what `goto` is genuinely for in C: it is the only way to get one cleanup path rather than a copy of the teardown at every early return, and copies are how a leak gets added later.

activities.title: What the standard says
activities.prompt: Match each expression to how the standard classifies it.
activities.explanation: The distinction is not academic. Because signed overflow is undefined, a compiler is entitled to optimize away a check written *after* the overflow — the check becomes dead code under the assumption the overflow never occurred. Unsigned arithmetic wraps predictably, which is why it is the right tool for hashing and bit manipulation.

pairs.right: Undefined — the compiler may assume it never happens
Defined — wraps modulo the type's range
Undefined in practice; the value is indeterminate

activities.title: Freeing what was allocated
activities.prompt: Complete this so the allocation is checked and released correctly.
activities.explanation: `sizeof *nums` stays correct if the type of `nums` ever changes, which `sizeof(int)` does not — the repeated type name is a second place to update and therefore a second place to forget. Checking for NULL is not optional: on failure `malloc` returns it, and writing through it is a crash at best.

blanks.hint: Size it from the thing being pointed at, not from a repeated type name.
What malloc returns on failure.

curricula.title: C#
curricula.summary: For someone who writes C# and has never had to think about what the runtime is doing underneath. About value and reference semantics, nullability, and asynchrony that is genuinely asynchronous.

activities.title: The call that hangs
activities.prompt: In a UI or classic ASP.NET application, why can `var x = GetAsync().Result;` deadlock?
activities.explanation: With a synchronization context, the continuation after an `await` is posted back to that single context thread. `.Result` is blocking that very thread, so the continuation can never run and the wait never ends. Await all the way up, or if you truly cannot, use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in the library so the continuation does not need that thread.

options.text: `.Result` blocks the context thread that the awaited continuation needs to resume on.
`.Result` starts the task a second time.
options.why: A task is started once. Accessing `.Result` waits for the one that exists.

options.text: The task is garbage collected while blocked.
options.why: A task being awaited is reachable, and collection would not present as a hang.

options.text: `.Result` throws unless the task has already completed.
options.why: It blocks until completion. It throws only for a faulted or canceled task.

activities.title: Null-conditional and coalescing
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `?.` short-circuits the whole chain: once the left side is null the rest is skipped and the expression is null, so `??` supplies the fallback. Note that the first line does not throw despite `.ToString()` appearing after `.Length` — short-circuiting covers the remainder of the chain, not just the next member.

activities.title: When the query runs
activities.prompt: `var q = items.Where(x => x.Active);` then `items.Add(newActiveItem);` then `q.Count()`. What does `Count()` see?
activities.explanation: LINQ operators are lazy: `Where` returns a query, and nothing is evaluated until something enumerates it. That is usually what you want, and occasionally a trap — a query held across a change, or enumerated twice, does the work twice. `ToList()` is how you say "run it now, once."

options.text: The item added after the query was written, because the query runs at Count().
Only the items present when `Where` was called.
options.why: `Where` builds a description; it does not capture a snapshot of the collection.

options.text: It throws, because the collection changed.
options.why: That happens when you modify a collection *during* enumeration, not before it starts.

options.text: Undefined behavior.
options.why: The semantics are specified and deterministic; deferred execution is a designed feature.

activities.title: The stream that stays open
activities.prompt: Which line leaves a handle open when the read throws?
activities.explanation: If `ReadEverything` throws, line 3 never runs and the file handle leaks. `using` ties disposal to the scope so it happens on every exit path, including exceptions. Manual `Dispose` at the end of a method is correct only when nothing between can fail, which is rarely worth reasoning about.

activities.title: Which kind of type
activities.prompt: Match each declaration to how equality and copying behave.
activities.explanation: Two independent choices are in play: how equality works and where the value lives. `record` changes the first, `struct` changes the second, and you can have either, both or neither. Reaching for `record` when you meant `struct` gives you sensible equality and unexpected aliasing.

pairs.right: Value equality and copying, with a generated ToString

activities.title: Passing cancellation through
activities.prompt: Complete the signature and the call so this work can actually be canceled.
activities.explanation: A cancellation token only does something if it reaches the call that is actually waiting. Accepting one and not forwarding it is worse than not accepting one at all, because the signature now promises cancellation that will never happen.

blanks.hint: The parameter type, by convention last.
Pass it on, every time.

curricula.title: C++
curricula.summary: For someone who writes C with classes and keeps meeting the parts that were added since. Built entirely around lifetime: what owns what, and what happens when it goes away.

skills.name: Copy, move, and the rule of zero
auto, and when it hides something

activities.title: Which pointer
activities.prompt: A parser owns a syntax tree. Nothing else outlives the parser. Which should hold the nodes?
activities.explanation: Single owner, clear lifetime, no runtime cost over a raw pointer, and correct on every exit path including exceptions. `shared_ptr` is for genuinely shared ownership; reaching for it because lifetime is unclear usually means the design question has been deferred rather than answered.

options.text: std::unique_ptr
std::shared_ptr
options.why: Shared ownership costs an atomic refcount and, worse, obscures the lifetime. Use it when ownership is genuinely shared, not as a default.

options.text: Raw new and delete
options.why: Correct only if every path frees exactly once, which includes every exception. That is what unique_ptr does for you.

options.text: A raw pointer to a static buffer
options.why: Fixes the lifetime problem by removing the ability to have more than one parser.

activities.title: A reference to a temporary
activities.prompt: This prints rubbish. Which line causes it?
activities.explanation: `full` is destroyed when the function returns, and the returned `string_view` points into it. A view never owns anything — it is a pointer and a length — so returning one that refers to a local is always wrong. Views are for parameters, where the caller's string outlives the call.
activities.correction: return full;  // with the return type changed to std::string

activities.title: After a move
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: A moved-from standard library object is left in a valid but unspecified state, and for `std::string` implementations in practice that is the empty string. "Valid but unspecified" means you may destroy it or assign to it, but you should not rely on what it contains — this prints 0 here and the standard does not promise it.

activities.title: What the compiler generates
activities.prompt: Match each declaration to its effect on the special member functions.
activities.explanation: This is why the rule of five exists: writing a destructor because your class owns something quietly turns every move into a copy, which is a performance bug with no diagnostic. If you declare one of the five, consider all of them — and prefer owning members that need none of it.

pairs.right: Generated, and the intent is documented

activities.title: Sliced on the way in
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: Passing by value copies the Animal *part* of the Dog into a fresh Animal — the Dog half is sliced off, and the call dispatches to the base implementation because the object genuinely is a base object now. The reference version keeps the original Dog, and the virtual call finds the override. activities.title: A reference to a corpse
activities.prompt: This compiles cleanly and is undefined behavior. Which line?

The view outlives its target and the print reads freed memory. string_view is a borrow with no borrow checker: it never owns, so every function returning one is making an unchecked promise about someone else's lifetime. activities.title: The iterator that stopped being valid

activities.title: What err is
activities.prompt: In Go, an error returned from a function is best described as which of these?
activities.explanation: `error` is an interface with one method. An error value is returned, stored and passed like any other value, and nothing forces you to look at it. That is the whole design: error handling is ordinary code, visible in the control flow, with no separate mechanism to learn.

options.text: An exception that unwinds the stack until something catches it.
options.why: Nothing unwinds. This is the model from other languages that makes Go's error handling feel verbose rather than deliberate.

options.text: An ordinary value of an interface type, returned alongside the result.
A special return slot the runtime checks for you.
options.why: The runtime checks nothing. If you ignore the value, it is ignored.

options.text: A status code that must be compared against zero.
options.why: Comparison is against `nil`, and `errors.Is` exists precisely because comparing directly is often wrong.

activities.title: Wrapping and unwrapping
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `%w` wraps: the new error carries the original inside it, so the message gains context while the identity survives. `errors.Is` walks that chain, which is why it reports true even though `err` is not `ErrNotFound` itself. Use `%w` when a caller might reasonably test for the cause, and `%v` when it is genuinely just a message.

activities.title: The nil that is not nil
activities.prompt: This function reports an error even when everything succeeded. Which line is at fault?
activities.explanation: Returning a nil `*MyError` as an `error` produces an interface value that is *not* nil: it has a type (`*MyError`) and a nil value, and `err != nil` is true. This is the classic Go trap. Either return the concrete type and let the caller decide, or return an explicit untyped `nil` when there is no error.

activities.prompt: What does this print?

b := a[:2]
b = append(b, 99)

activities.explanation: A pointer can reach a value method, but a value cannot reach a pointer method, because there may be no address to take. So `*T` always has the larger method set. When an interface assignment fails and the method is plainly there, this is almost always why.

activities.title: Loose, strict, and Object.is
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `==` converts before comparing, and the conversions are not the ones intuition suggests: `''` becomes `0`, and `[]` becomes `''` and then `0`. `===` compares without converting and is the default for that reason. `NaN` is the one value not equal to itself under both, which is why `array.indexOf(NaN)` never finds anything and `Object.is` exists.

activities.title: The default that eats a zero
activities.prompt: A settings form stores `{ retries: 0 }`. Which expression returns `0` rather than the fallback?
activities.explanation: `??` falls back only for `null` and `undefined` — "no value was supplied" — while `||` falls back for the whole falsy list, which includes `0`, `''` and `false`. Every one of those is a real answer somebody meant: a quantity of zero, a search box deliberately cleared, a setting explicitly turned off. The bug is quiet, the replacement value is plausible, and nothing throws.

settings.retries || 3
options.why: `||` falls back for every falsy value, and `0` is falsy. This is the bug the question is about.

options.why: Same test as `||`, written out longer.

activities.prompt: This is meant to leave `defaults` untouched and does not. Which line changes it?
activities.explanation: `const` freezes the *binding*, not the object. `merged` is a second name for the same object, so `Object.assign` writes straight through into `defaults` and every later call starts from the previous call's overrides. Spreading into a fresh object copies the properties instead, which is what "merge" was supposed to mean.

activities.title: The callback that lost its object
activities.prompt: `setTimeout(counter.tick, 100)` reports `undefined` where `counter.tick()` works. Why?
activities.explanation: `counter.tick()` calls with `counter` as the receiver. `counter.tick` alone is just the function, and by the time setTimeout calls it there is no object on the left of the dot, so `this` is undefined in a module. `counter.tick.bind(counter)` or `() => counter.tick()` keeps the receiver. An arrow method defined in the class body has no `this` of its own and closes over the instance, which is why that style exists.

setTimeout runs the function in a different scope.

options.why: Nothing here is asynchronous in a way that would matter, and `async` does not affect `this`.

options.text: `counter` is out of scope by then.
options.why: The closure holds it. The reference survives; the receiver does not.

activities.title: Which of these copy
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `sort` mutates in place and returns the same array, so `items` is now sorted and `sorted` is not a copy — the commonest surprise in the array API, and the reason `toSorted` was added. `map` returns a new array and leaves the original alone. Knowing which methods mutate is most of using arrays correctly: `push`, `splice`, `reverse` and `sort` do; `map`, `filter`, `slice` and `concat` do not.

activities.title: Handling a failure without swallowing it
activities.prompt: Put these in order so a failed fetch reports its status rather than throwing a type error.
activities.explanation: `fetch` rejects only when the request could not be made at all. A 404 or a 500 resolves perfectly happily with `ok: false`, so code that goes straight to `.json()` tries to parse an error page and fails with something about unexpected tokens — a message pointing at JSON when the real problem was the status. Checking `ok` first is the whole fix, and it is the single most skipped line in front-end code.

activities.title: Sequential when it did not need to be
activities.prompt: Three independent fetches take three seconds in total, one second each. What makes them take one?
activities.explanation: Each `await` suspends until that promise settles, so three of them in a row is three round trips end to end. `Promise.all` starts all three immediately and waits for the slowest, which is the actual dependency. The rule is simple: `await` in sequence only when the next call *needs* the previous result. `Promise.allSettled` is the variant to reach for when one failure should not discard the other two answers.

options.why: Then the values are promises rather than results, and everything downstream breaks.

options.text: Marking the enclosing function async.
options.why: It already is — `await` is only legal inside one.

options.text: Running them in a for loop.
options.why: A loop with an await inside is exactly as sequential, and often accidentally so.

activities.title: Imports and exports
activities.prompt: Match each export to the import that reaches it.
activities.explanation: A default export has no name of its own, so the importing side invents one — which is why two files can import the same default under different names and why renaming the function changes nothing for its callers. Named exports are checked: import a name that does not exist and the module fails to load rather than handing you `undefined` at the point of use.

activities.title: A counter that keeps its own state
activities.prompt: Complete this so each call to `makeCounter()` gets its own independent count.
activities.explanation: The returned function closes over `count`, and each call to `makeCounter` creates a fresh one — so two counters never interfere. Declaring it outside the factory would make one shared variable and every counter would advance together, which is the bug this shape exists to prevent. `const` fails here for the ordinary reason: the value is reassigned.

activities.title: Adding, and what it means
activities.prompt: What is `[] + {}`, and what is `1 + '1'`?
activities.explanation: `+` is overloaded: numeric addition when both sides are numbers, string concatenation the moment either is a string. Every other arithmetic operator only means arithmetic, which is why `'3' * 2` is 6 while `'3' + 2` is `'32'`. The practical rule is to convert explicitly at the boundary — `Number(input)` — rather than letting a form value stay a string and discovering it four lines later.

An error, and 2.

options.text: '[object Object]' and 2.

activities.title: What the broker actually promises
activities.prompt: A queue advertises "exactly-once delivery". What does a consumer still have to do?
activities.explanation: Between receiving a message, performing a side effect and acknowledging it, there is a window where a crash means the work happened and the acknowledgement did not. The message is redelivered and the work happens twice. No broker closes that window, so the consumer must be safe to run twice — usually a key, recorded transactionally with the effect.

options.text: Be idempotent, because exactly-once processing is what you need and no broker can give it to you end to end.
Nothing further; that is what the guarantee means.
options.why: The guarantee covers the broker's own handoff. It cannot cover the side effects your handler performs before acknowledging.

options.text: Acknowledge before processing.
options.why: That converts a crash into a lost message — at-most-once, which is usually worse than a duplicate.

options.text: Disable retries.
options.why: Then a transient failure loses the message permanently.

activities.explanation: The state change and the intent to publish commit together, so there is no moment where one exists without the other. Publishing directly inside the transaction is the trap: the broker call can succeed and the transaction still roll back, announcing something that never happened. activities.explanation: Head-of-line blocking is the failure mode: one bad message stops everything behind it. A DLQ bounds the damage to that message and turns a total stall into an alert plus one item to look at. It is only useful if somebody actually watches it — an unmonitored DLQ is a directory where data goes to be forgotten.

options.text: Taking the message out of the way after N attempts so the rest can proceed, while keeping it for inspection.
Deleting messages that fail.

options.text: Retrying more slowly.

options.text: Storing messages during an outage.
options.why: The main queue does that. A DLQ holds things that have already failed repeatedly.

Generate it at the edge if the caller did not supply one, put it in every log line, and pass it on every outbound call — including into queue messages, which is the hop people forget.

activities.title: Ordering
activities.prompt: In what order do these print?
activities.explanation: Synchronous code finishes first, so `a` and `e`. Then the microtask queues drain before the loop continues, and `process.nextTick` runs ahead of promise callbacks. `setTimeout` is a timer phase of the loop proper, so it comes last despite the zero. activities.title: Why pipe rather than read-then-write
activities.prompt: Copying a 4 GB file with `writeFileSync(dest, readFileSync(src))` fails on a small container. What does piping change?

A pipeline moves it in chunks and — the part that matters — applies back pressure: when the destination cannot keep up the source pauses. Use `pipeline()` rather than `.pipe()` so that an error anywhere destroys every stream instead of leaking the ones still open.

options.text: It moves the data in chunks and stops reading when the writer falls behind.
It is the same operation with less code.
options.why: It is a materially different operation; the resource profile is the entire point.

options.text: It uses a background thread, so the memory is not counted.

options.text: It compresses the data in transit.

A constant, with a comment saying to change it before deploying.

activities.prompt: Complete the f-string so it prints `Total: 1,234.50`.
activities.explanation: The format spec after the colon is the same mini-language `format()` uses. `,` inserts thousands separators, `.2f` fixes two decimal places, and the order matters — `:,.2f`, not `:.2f,`. Reaching for string concatenation and manual rounding instead is how a total ends up displayed as `1234.5000000001`.
activities.template:
total = 1234.5
print(f"Total: {total{1}}")

blanks.hint: A colon starts the format spec; a comma groups thousands.

activities.title: The line that always runs
activities.prompt: This reports success even when the check fails. Which line is at fault?
activities.explanation: `print("saved")` is at module level, not inside `save`, so it runs once when the file is imported and never again. In a language with braces this would be a misplaced brace and probably a syntax error; in Python it is valid code that does something else entirely, which is why indentation here is structure rather than style.
activities.code:
def save(record):
    if record.get("id") is None:
        print("no id")
        return False
    write(record)
    return True
print("saved")
activities.correction: print("saved")  # inside the function, after write

activities.title: What each import brings in
activities.prompt: Match each import to the name it makes available.
activities.explanation: `import x` binds the module; `from x import y` binds the member and not the module. The practical difference is at the call site — `json.dumps` says where it came from, `dumps` does not — which is why the first form is the default in most style guides and the second is reserved for names that are unambiguous on their own.

pairs.left: from json import dumps as to_json

activities.title: Truthy, and what is not
activities.prompt: Which of these is truthy?
activities.explanation: Emptiness is what makes a container falsy, not what it contains. `[0]` has one element, so it is truthy, even though that element is falsy itself. This matters most when checking a function's return: `if items:` asks "is there anything", while `if items is not None:` asks "did I get a list at all", and confusing the two turns an empty result into an error case.

options.why: An empty list is falsy. A list containing a falsy value is not.
Zero is falsy, in every numeric type.
The empty string is falsy; a string of whitespace is not.

activities.title: What survives the loop
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: A `for` variable is not scoped to the loop — it survives afterwards, holding the last value it took. That is occasionally useful and more often a bug, because a loop that never ran leaves the name *unbound* entirely, and `print(i)` after an empty range raises `NameError` rather than printing anything.
activities.code:
for i in range(3):
    pass
print(i)

total = 0
for n in []:
    total += n
print(total)

activities.title: The else nobody expects
activities.prompt: When does the `else` on a `for` loop run?
activities.explanation: Read it as "no break" rather than "else", and it stops being strange: the block runs when the search ended without finding anything. It replaces the `found = False` flag that this pattern otherwise needs, and it is the one piece of Python syntax that regularly surprises people who have written the language for years.

options.text: When the loop finished without hitting a break.
When the loop body never ran.
options.why: That is one case where it runs, but not the rule — it also runs after a loop that completed normally.

options.text: When the loop raised an exception.
options.why: An exception propagates; the else is skipped along with everything after it.

options.text: Every time, after the loop.
options.why: A `break` skips it, which is the entire reason the construct exists.

activities.title: Indexing without a counter
activities.prompt: Put these in order to print each name with its one-based position.
activities.explanation: `enumerate` yields the index alongside the value, and its `start` argument moves the numbering without arithmetic at the call site. The alternative — `for i in range(len(names))` and then `names[i]` — is longer, indexes twice, and is the single clearest signal in a code review that somebody is writing another language in Python's syntax.
lines: for position, name in enumerate(names, start=1):

activities.title: The loop that never ends
activities.prompt: This never terminates. Which line is missing the work?
activities.explanation: `continue` jumps straight back to the condition, skipping the decrement below it. On the first even value the counter stops moving and the loop runs forever printing the same number. `continue` in a `while` is the one place it is genuinely dangerous: in a `for` loop the iterator still advances, so the same mistake terminates.

activities.title: Multiplying a list of lists
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `* 3` repeats the *reference*, not the list. All three rows are the same object, so writing through one is visible through all of them. The inner `[0] * 2` is fine because integers are immutable — the problem only appears when the repeated element is mutable. `[[0] * 2 for _ in range(3)]` builds three separate rows, and is the reason that comprehension is the idiom for a grid.
activities.code:
grid = [[0] * 2] * 3
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)

activities.title: Absent, or present and None
activities.prompt: `settings = {"retries": None}`. Which expression distinguishes a missing key from a key whose value is `None`?
activities.explanation: `in` asks about the key; everything else asks about the value. The distinction matters whenever `None` is a legitimate stored value — a setting explicitly turned off, a field deliberately cleared — because `get` collapses "absent" and "present and empty" into one answer. A sentinel object is the other way: `settings.get(key, MISSING)`.

options.text: "retries" in settings
settings.get("retries")
options.why: Returns None for both cases, which is exactly the ambiguity being asked about.

options.text: settings.get("retries") is not None
options.why: False for both, for the same reason.

options.text: bool(settings["retries"])
options.why: Raises for a missing key and returns False for a stored None — two different failures, neither of them an answer.

activities.title: Changing a dictionary while reading it
activities.prompt: This raises at run time. Which line causes it?
activities.explanation: A dictionary cannot change size while it is being iterated; Python detects it and raises `RuntimeError` rather than quietly skipping entries. Wrapping the keys in `list()` takes a snapshot first, so the loop iterates over that and the deletions land on the dictionary. The same rule applies to sets, and to lists you are removing from by index.

activities.title: Slices that cannot fail
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: A slice is half-open — it includes the start and excludes the stop — so `items[1:3]` has two elements, and `items[:n]` and `items[n:]` partition the list with no overlap and no gap. Out-of-range slices clamp rather than raise, which is why `items[10:20]` is empty while `items[10]` would be an `IndexError`. The step of `-1` reverses.
activities.code:
items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(items[1:3])
print(items[:2])
print(items[-2:])
print(items[10:20])
print(items[::-1])

activities.title: Filter and reshape in one pass
activities.prompt: Complete the comprehension so it produces the upper-cased names of the active users only.
activities.explanation: The order reads awkwardly at first and is fixed: the expression comes first, then the `for`, then the `if`. It is deliberately the same order as a nested loop with the body hoisted to the front, which is why multiple `for` clauses in one comprehension read left to right like nested loops rather than inside out.
activities.template:
users = [{"name": "ada", "active": True}, {"name": "bob", "active": False}]
names = [user["name"].upper() {1} user in users {2} user["active"]]

blanks.hint: What drives the iteration.
What decides whether an item is kept.

activities.title: Set operations
activities.prompt: Given a = {1, 2, 3} and b = {3, 4}, match each expression to its value.
activities.explanation: Union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference. The reason to reach for a set at all is the third one: "which of these are not in that" is a loop with an `in` check over a list — quadratic — and a single operation on sets, which is linear. Membership in a set is constant time and in a list is not, and that is usually the whole performance story.

activities.title: When a tuple is the right answer
activities.prompt: Which of these genuinely requires a tuple rather than a list?
activities.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable, and a list is not, precisely because it can change — a key that could mutate after insertion would be lost in the table. A tuple of hashable things is hashable, which is what makes `counts[(row, column)]` work and `counts[[row, column]]` a `TypeError`. Everything else about tuples is convention.

options.text: Using the value as a dictionary key.
Returning two values from a function.
options.why: Works with either; the tuple is idiomatic, but a list would function.

options.text: Iterating over a fixed sequence.
options.why: Both iterate identically.

options.text: Storing a large number of items.
options.why: A tuple is marginally smaller, which is almost never the reason to pick one.

activities.title: Sorting by a key
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: Python's sort is stable, so equal keys keep their original relative order — which is why `ada` still precedes `cy` in the first line. The second shows the idiom for sorting by several fields in different directions: a tuple key, with a negated number to reverse just that one. `reverse=True` would flip the names as well, which is usually not what is meant.
activities.code:
people = [("ada", 36), ("bob", 25), ("cy", 36)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))

activities.title: Counting without a dictionary of your own
activities.prompt: Put these in order to print the three commonest words.
activities.explanation: `Counter` is a dictionary that starts every key at zero and knows how to rank itself. The hand-written version — a dict, a `get(word, 0) + 1`, and a `sorted(..., key=..., reverse=True)[:3]` — is four more lines and one more place to get the tie-breaking wrong.

activities.title: Grouping records
activities.prompt: Complete this so each city maps to a list of the people living there.
activities.explanation: `defaultdict(list)` takes the *callable*, not `list()`: it is invoked once per missing key, so passing an instance would share one list between every group — the same aliasing trap as `[[0] * 2] * 3`. This replaces the `if key not in d: d[key] = []` preamble that otherwise begins every grouping loop.
activities.template:
from collections import defaultdict

by_city = defaultdict({1})
for person in people:
    by_city[person["city"]].{2}(person["name"])

blanks.hint: The factory called for a missing key — the type, not an instance.
Adding one item to the end of a list.

activities.title: The default that remembers
activities.prompt: The second call returns two items rather than one. Which line is wrong?
activities.explanation: A default argument is evaluated once, when the function is defined, not on each call. So every call that omits `into` shares one list, and it accumulates across calls for the life of the process. The fix is the standard idiom: default to `None` and build the real default inside. This applies to every mutable default — lists, dicts, sets — and to anything whose value is computed at definition time, such as `datetime.now()`.
activities.code:
def collect(item, into=[]):
    into.append(item)
    return into

print(collect("a"))
print(collect("b"))
activities.correction: def collect(item, into=None):  # then: if into is None: into = []

activities.title: What a dict remembers
activities.prompt: In Python 3.7 and later, iterating a dictionary yields its keys in which order?
activities.explanation: Insertion order became a language guarantee in 3.7, having been an implementation detail in 3.6. It means a dictionary built from a file round-trips in the same order, which makes output diffable and tests stable. Re-inserting an existing key does *not* move it to the end — only deleting and re-adding does.

options.text: The order they were first inserted.
Sorted order.
options.why: Nothing sorts them. That is `sorted(d)`, which is a different thing and costs more.

options.text: An arbitrary order that may change between runs.
options.why: True before 3.7, and the reason a lot of older advice says to sort before printing.

options.text: Reverse insertion order.
options.why: `reversed(d)` gives that, from 3.8 onwards.

activities.title: Positional, keyword, and the star
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `*tags` collects the extra positional arguments into a tuple — empty when there are none, never `None`. Anything after it is keyword-only, which is why `level` cannot be passed positionally however hard you try. `**extra` collects the keywords that no parameter claimed. The ordering rule is fixed: positional, `*args`, keyword-only, `**kwargs`.
activities.code:
def report(name, *tags, level="info", **extra):
    print(name, tags, level, extra)

report("a")
report("a", "x", "y", level="warn")
report("a", key=1)

activities.title: The name that is not there yet
activities.prompt: What happens when this runs?
activities.explanation: Python decides a name's scope by looking at the whole function body before running any of it. One assignment anywhere makes the name local *throughout*, including on the line that reads it first — so the read happens before the local has a value and raises `UnboundLocalError`. `global total` fixes it and is almost always the wrong fix; passing the value in and returning the new one is the right one.
activities.code:
total = 0

def add(n):
    total = total + n
    return total

add(5)

options.text: UnboundLocalError, because assigning to `total` makes it local everywhere in the function.
It returns 5 and leaves the global at 0.
options.why: That would be true if the function only *read* the global. The assignment changes the name's scope for the whole function body.

options.text: It returns 5 and sets the global to 5.
options.why: Python never rebinds a global from a function without `global` or `nonlocal`.

options.text: NameError, because `total` is not defined.
options.why: It is defined — at module level. The error is about scope, not existence, and Python distinguishes them.

activities.title: The except that hides the bug
activities.prompt: A typo in this function is invisible in production. Which line hides it?
activities.explanation: `except Exception` catches the `KeyError` from the misspelled key exactly as it would catch a genuine bad value, and returns 0 either way. Every score silently becomes zero and nothing is logged. Catching the two failures you actually expect leaves the typo to raise, which is what you want — a crash on the first request is far cheaper than a month of quietly wrong numbers.

activities.title: What a custom exception buys
activities.prompt: Why define `class InsufficientFunds(Exception)` rather than raising `ValueError("insufficient funds")`?
activities.explanation: The value is in what the caller can do. `except ValueError` around a transfer catches the insufficient-funds case *and* a malformed amount and a bad date, and cannot tell them apart without matching on the message — which breaks the first time anyone improves the wording. A named class is a stable thing to catch, and it makes the failure part of the API rather than an implementation detail.

options.text: A caller can catch this one case without catching every other ValueError.
It produces a better message.
options.why: The message is whatever you pass either way.

options.text: It is faster.
options.why: Exception classes cost the same. Performance is never the argument for one.

options.text: It prevents the error.
options.why: Naming a failure does not stop it happening.

activities.title: A record with equality
activities.prompt: Complete this so two accounts with the same fields compare equal and neither field can be reassigned.
activities.explanation: `@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__`, which is most of what a plain class was for. `frozen=True` adds immutability and, with it, `__hash__` — so a frozen dataclass can be a dictionary key or go in a set, and a mutable one cannot. Equality is by field value, which is almost always what a record means and never what a plain class does by default.

blanks.hint: Makes instances immutable — and hashable as a consequence.

activities.title: Where the state should live
activities.prompt: Match each design smell to what it usually means.
activities.explanation: The second is the one that causes real bugs: a total kept beside the items it totals will disagree with them the first time somebody adds a code path that updates one and not the other. Anything derivable should be computed on read. The last is the state-machine smell — an `is_draft` checked at the top of nine methods is usually a `Draft` and a `Published` that share an interface.

pairs.left: A method that reads no self
A flag checked in every method

activities.title: Lazy, and consumed once
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: A generator is an iterator, not a collection: it yields each value once and then it is exhausted. The second `sum` finds nothing left and returns 0 — no error, no warning, just a wrong answer, which is why this is worth meeting deliberately rather than in production. When a sequence has to be traversed twice, build a list.
activities.code:
squares = (n * n for n in range(4))
print(sum(squares))
print(sum(squares))
print(list(n * n for n in range(4)))

activities.title: A context manager of your own
activities.prompt: Put these in order to make a timer that reports even when the body raises.
activities.explanation: Everything before the `yield` is the setup, everything after is the teardown, and the `try/finally` is what makes the teardown run when the body raises. Without it the timer prints nothing on the one occasion you most want to know how long something took before it failed — which is the whole reason `with` exists rather than a pair of calls.

activities.title: The decorator that eats the name
activities.prompt: After decorating with this, `greet.__name__` is `"wrapper"` rather than `"greet"`. What fixes it?
activities.explanation: A decorator replaces the function with the wrapper, so every piece of metadata — name, docstring, signature, module — becomes the wrapper's. `functools.wraps` copies them across, and it is one line. Leaving it out is how a codebase ends up with a traceback in which nine frames are all called `wrapper`.

options.text: `@functools.wraps(function)` on the wrapper.
Returning `function` instead of `wrapper`.
options.why: That removes the decoration entirely — the logging never happens.

options.text: Setting `wrapper.__name__ = "greet"`.
options.why: Works for one function and hard-codes a name the decorator cannot know.

options.text: Nothing; the name is unimportant.
options.why: It is what `help()`, tracebacks, pickling and most debuggers report. A wall of `wrapper` in a stack trace is a real cost.

activities.title: Saying what might be missing
activities.prompt: Complete the annotation so the signature admits that a lookup can fail.
activities.explanation: `str | None` says what `Optional[str]` used to and reads better. The point is not the syntax: a function that can return `None` and does not say so is one every caller will eventually forget to check, and a type checker cannot warn about a possibility the signature denies. Annotating the failure is what turns "it crashed in production" into "it did not compile".
activities.template:
def find_user(users: dict[str, str], key: str) -> str {1} None:
    return users.get(key)

blanks.hint: The union operator, since 3.10.

activities.title: What makes a test worth having
activities.prompt: Which of these is the strongest reason a test is not pulling its weight?
activities.explanation: A test that passes against a broken implementation is measuring nothing, and it is worse than no test because it reports green. This is the idea behind the mutation gate in this repository: the reference solution is deliberately damaged, and any fault the tests fail to notice is a hole in the suite rather than a fact about the learner.

options.text: It still passes when the function it tests is deliberately broken.
It is only three lines long.
options.why: Length says nothing. A three-line test of the right thing beats thirty lines of setup.

options.text: It has no docstring.
options.why: A well-named test needs no docstring, and one does not make a weak test strong.

options.text: It duplicates part of another test.
options.why: Some overlap is fine and occasionally deliberate — an edge case worth asserting twice.

activities.title: The recursion that never stops
activities.prompt: This overflows the stack on any input. Which line is wrong?
activities.explanation: The base case is right and unreachable: nothing moves `n` toward it, so every call makes an identical one. A recursive function needs both a stop and *progress toward it*, and the missing half is nearly always the second. Python's default limit is a thousand frames, so this fails fast — which is a kindness compared with a language that would simply crash.

activities.title: What memoization actually changes
activities.prompt: `fib` is the naive two-call recursion, `fast` is the same function with `@lru_cache`. How many calls does each make for n = 30? Answer as `naive|cached`, using the order of growth rather than exact numbers.
activities.explanation: The naive version recomputes the same subproblems over and over — about 1.6 to the n calls, which is roughly 2.7 million for n = 30. The cache makes each distinct n happen once, so the work becomes linear and the whole thing returns instantly. This is the entire idea behind dynamic programming: the recursion was already correct, and only the repetition was expensive.

activities.title: What each lookup costs
activities.prompt: Match each operation to its cost on a container of n items.
activities.explanation: The first two are the whole reason sets exist, and swapping one for the other turns a loop from linear into quadratic without changing a line of logic — the commonest single performance bug in Python. `insert(0, x)` is the other trap: it shifts every element, so building a list by prepending is quadratic where `append` plus one `reverse` is linear. `collections.deque` prepends in constant time.

pairs.right: linear — scans until it finds it

activities.title: The queue that is not one
activities.prompt: A breadth-first search uses `queue.pop(0)` on a list and gets slower than expected on large graphs. Why?
activities.explanation: A list is contiguous, so removing the front means moving everything after it down one. Doing that once per node makes an otherwise linear traversal quadratic. `collections.deque` has `popleft` in constant time and is the right container for a queue — the change is one import and one method name, and on a large graph it is the difference between seconds and minutes.

options.text: `pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, so the traversal becomes quadratic.
Lists cannot hold enough items.
options.why: A Python list will hold as much as memory allows; the problem is the cost per operation, not the capacity.

options.text: BFS is inherently quadratic.
options.why: BFS visits each node and edge once. The quadratic term comes entirely from the container.

options.text: `pop(0)` copies the list.
options.why: It shifts in place rather than copying, which is cheaper and still linear.

activities.title: The binary search that loops
activities.prompt: This hangs when the target is absent. Which line is at fault?
activities.explanation: Without the `+ 1` the window stops shrinking as soon as `low` and `high` are adjacent: `middle` computes to `low`, the branch sets `low = middle`, and nothing has changed. Every bound must move strictly past the value just examined, because that value has been ruled out. Binary search is four lines and famously hard to get right; this is the way it is usually wrong.

activities.title: Which traversal finds the shortest path
activities.prompt: On an unweighted graph, which traversal finds the fewest-edges path, and why?
activities.explanation: Breadth-first expands in rings of equal distance, so the first time it reaches a node it has arrived by a fewest-edges route and can never do better later. That is why the visited set can be marked on *enqueue* rather than on dequeue. The moment edges have differing weights the argument collapses and Dijkstra's priority queue replaces the plain queue.

options.text: Breadth-first, because it reaches every node at distance k before any at k + 1.
Depth-first, because it explores each branch fully.
options.why: DFS finds *a* path, and there is no reason it is the shortest — it commits to the first branch and may reach the target the long way round.

options.text: Either; they visit the same nodes.
options.why: They visit the same nodes in different orders, and the order is exactly what decides which path is found first.

options.text: Neither: shortest paths need Dijkstra.
options.why: Dijkstra is for weighted edges. With every edge costing one, it degenerates into breadth-first.

activities.title: Two ends, one pass
activities.prompt: Complete this so it finds a pair summing to `target` in a sorted list, in one pass.
activities.explanation: Sortedness is what makes this work: if the sum is too small then no pair using the current low value can help, because every remaining partner is smaller than the one just tried. Each step discards a whole row of the pair space, so the scan is linear where the nested loop is quadratic. It is the same argument as binary search, applied from both ends.

blanks.hint: The sum is too small, so the smaller end must grow.
The sum is too large, so the larger end must shrink.

activities.title: When dynamic programming is the answer
activities.prompt: Which pair of properties makes a problem suit dynamic programming?
activities.explanation: Both halves are needed. Overlap is what makes memoization pay — merge sort recurses beautifully and its subproblems never repeat, so caching buys nothing. Optimal substructure is what makes combining sub-answers valid; where it fails, the best overall answer may not be built from the best pieces, and the recurrence is simply wrong however fast it runs.

options.text: Overlapping subproblems, and an optimal answer built from optimal sub-answers.
A large input and a slow solution.
options.why: That describes wanting a better algorithm, not this one. Plenty of slow problems have no useful subproblem structure at all.

options.text: Recursion and a base case.
options.why: Every recursion has those. Without *overlap* there is nothing for a cache to save.

options.text: Sorted input and a monotonic answer.
options.why: That is the shape binary search and two-pointer exploit.

activities.title: The classic
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: Neither 0.1 nor 0.2 is representable in binary floating point, so their sum lands a hair above 0.3. This is not a Python quirk — it is IEEE 754, and every language with doubles does it. Compare with a tolerance, or use `Decimal` where the values are decimal by nature. Money is the obvious case: it should be integer pence or `Decimal`, never a float.
activities.code:
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 10) == 0.3)
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))

activities.title: The tools worth knowing
activities.prompt: Match each helper to the hand-written loop it replaces.
activities.explanation: `groupby` is the one that catches people out: it groups *adjacent* equal keys, not all equal keys, so it does what SQL's GROUP BY does only if the input is sorted by that key first. Unsorted input produces several small groups for the same key, silently and plausibly — which is exactly the kind of wrong answer that survives a code review.
