activities.title: How to hold a graph
activities.prompt: A social graph has a million people and about a hundred friends each. Adjacency list or adjacency matrix?
activities.explanation: Density decides it. A matrix costs n² regardless of how many edges exist, which is right for a dense graph and ruinous for a sparse one — and almost every real graph is sparse. An adjacency list costs n + e and gives you a node's neighbors directly, which is what a traversal actually asks for. The matrix wins when you need "is there an edge between these two" constantly on a small dense graph.

options.text: A list — the matrix would need a trillion cells, almost all empty.
A matrix, because edge lookup is constant.
options.why: True and unaffordable: a million squared is 10^12 cells for 10^8 edges.

options.text: Either; the difference is small.
options.why: The difference is four orders of magnitude in memory here.

options.text: A matrix, because the graph is undirected.
options.why: Direction affects neither choice; density does.

curricula.title: React
curricula.summary: For someone who can already write JavaScript and keeps being surprised by when a component runs. About rendering as a function of state, and about the escape hatches you should almost never need.

skills.name: JSX, and what it compiles to
Derived state, and not storing it
The rules, and why they exist

activities.title: The list that will not re-render
activities.prompt: Adding an item does nothing on screen. Which line is at fault?
activities.explanation: `push` mutates the array that state already holds, so when `setItems` is called with that same array React compares it to the previous value, sees the identical reference, and skips the render. State must be replaced, not edited. The fix is one new array; the habit is worth more than the fix.

activities.title: Two increments
activities.prompt: `count` starts at 0. The button is clicked once. What does the next render show?
activities.explanation: `count` is a value captured by this render, and it is 0 for both calls, so both queue "set it to 1". Writing `setCount(c => c + 1)` instead passes a function that receives the latest queued value, and two of those give 2. This is the difference between reading state and describing a change to it.

activities.title: Why the effect never re-runs
activities.prompt: An effect fetches a user by `userId`, but changing `userId` never refetches. The dependency array is `[]`. What is actually wrong?
activities.explanation: A dependency array is a claim: "nothing else this effect reads can change." Leaving `userId` out makes that claim false, so React honors it and never re-runs. The array is not a performance knob, it is a description of the effect's inputs, and a wrong description produces a component that renders stale data with no error anywhere.

options.text: The array should list `userId`, because it is read inside the effect.
The array should be omitted entirely so the effect always runs.
options.why: That runs it after every render, which refetches on unrelated state changes and can loop forever.

options.text: The effect should be wrapped in `useCallback`.
options.why: `useCallback` memoises a function; it has no bearing on when an effect re-runs.

options.text: State updates cannot trigger effects.
options.why: They can, and do — that is the entire mechanism being asked about.

activities.title: When not to use an effect
activities.prompt: You have `items` in state and want `total`, the sum. Which is right?
activities.explanation: Anything derivable from existing state is not state. Computing it during render means it can never be out of date, needs no synchronization, and deletes a whole class of bug. Reach for `useMemo` only when the computation is genuinely expensive, and never for correctness.

options.text: An effect watching `items` that calls `setTotal`.
options.why: This renders twice for every change and creates a window where total disagrees with items. It is the commonest unnecessary effect.

options.text: Compute it during render: `const total = items.reduce(...)`.
Store `total` alongside `items` and update both everywhere.
options.why: Two sources of truth for one fact, which will drift the first time somebody adds a code path.

options.text: A `useMemo` with no dependency array.
options.why: Without a dependency array `useMemo` recomputes every render — the same as computing it directly, but with more words.

activities.title: What each hook is for
activities.prompt: Match each hook to the job it exists to do.
activities.explanation: The distinction that matters most is the first two: `useRef` is the escape hatch for something you need to remember but must not trigger a render — a timer id, a DOM node, the previous value. Using state for those causes render loops; using a ref for real state causes a screen that never updates.

curricula.title: Rust
curricula.summary: For someone who has bounced off the borrow checker. Built around making ownership feel like a description of what your program already does rather than a tax on writing it.

skills.name: When cloning is the right answer

activities.title: Where the string went
activities.prompt: What does the compiler say about this program?
activities.explanation: Assigning a `String` moves it. After `let b = a`, the value belongs to `b` and `a` is no longer usable — not emptied, not freed, just no longer a name you are allowed to use. The compiler rejects the program rather than leaving you two owners of one heap allocation, which is the double-free this rule exists to prevent.

options.text: It prints `hello`.
options.why: This is what happens in almost every other language, which is exactly why it is the wrong answer here.

options.text: It does not compile: borrow of moved value `a`.
It prints an empty string, because `a` was emptied.
options.why: Nothing is emptied. `a` is still the same bytes; the compiler has simply stopped letting you name them.

options.text: It compiles but the behavior is undefined.
options.why: Rust's entire proposition is that this class of mistake is a compile error rather than undefined behavior.

activities.title: Making the error go away
activities.prompt: This does not compile. Which change is the one to reach for *first*, if you only need to read `a` afterwards?
activities.explanation: Borrowing is the cheap answer and usually the right one. `&a` gives `b` a reference — permission to read, no transfer of ownership — so `a` stays usable and nothing is copied. Reach for `clone` when you genuinely need a second independent value, not to silence the compiler.

options.text: `let b = a.clone();`
options.why: It works, and it copies the whole string to do it. Correct but wasteful when nobody needed a second copy.

options.text: `let b = &a;`
Wrap it: `let a = Rc::new(String::from("hello"));`
options.why: Reference counting solves shared *ownership*. Nothing here needs shared ownership; it needs a look.

options.text: Make it mutable: `let mut a = ...`
options.why: Mutability and ownership are different rules. `mut` has no bearing on whether a value has been moved.

activities.title: Two borrows
activities.prompt: One line here makes the program illegal. Which one?
activities.explanation: `first` is an immutable borrow of the vector, and it is still alive on the last line. `push` needs a mutable borrow, and Rust allows either one mutable borrow or any number of immutable ones, never both. This is not pedantry: `push` may reallocate, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory. The rule is the reason that cannot happen.

activities.title: What each one gives you back
activities.prompt: Match each expression on an `Option<i32>` to what it evaluates to.
activities.explanation: `unwrap_or` leaves the `Option` behind and hands you a value, substituting a default for `None`. `map` stays inside the `Option`: it applies the function if there is something there and does nothing if there is not. Knowing which of the two you want is most of working with `Option`.

activities.title: The question mark
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: `?` unwraps a `Result` when it is `Ok` and returns early with the error when it is not. So the first call reaches `Ok(n * 2)` with `n` at 21, and the second never gets past the `?` — the `ParseIntError` is returned from `parse` unchanged. It is an early return, not exception handling.

activities.title: A function that only reads
activities.prompt: Complete the signature so `longest_name` can read the list without taking it away from the caller.
activities.explanation: Taking `&Vec<String>` borrows the list: the caller can still use it after the call. Returning `&str` hands back a slice pointing into a string the vector still owns, which is sound precisely because the borrow of the vector outlives the call. Take ownership only when you intend to keep or consume the value.

curricula.title: SQL
curricula.summary: For someone who writes queries that work and cannot say why the slow one is slow. About sets, joins, and reading a query plan.

skills.name: Types, and what the database refuses

activities.title: Counting the missing
activities.prompt: A `people` table has 10 rows. Three have a NULL `email`. What does `SELECT COUNT(email) FROM people` return?
activities.explanation: `COUNT(column)` counts non-NULL values; `COUNT(*)` counts rows. The gap between them is the number of missing values, and mistaking one for the other is one of the quietest ways to publish a wrong number.

options.why: This is what `COUNT(*)` returns. The difference between the two is exactly this question.
Nothing counts only the NULLs; you would need `COUNT(*) - COUNT(email)`.

options.text: NULL
options.why: Aggregates do not become NULL because their input contains NULLs.

activities.title: The filter that undoes the join
activities.prompt: Why does this return no rows for customers with no orders?
activities.explanation: The LEFT JOIN does keep unmatched customers, filling `o.total` with NULL. Then WHERE evaluates `NULL > 100`, which is unknown, not true, so those rows are dropped and the LEFT JOIN has been silently turned into an inner one. Put the condition in the ON clause, or test for NULL explicitly.
activities.code:
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.total > 100;

options.text: LEFT JOIN only keeps rows that match, so unmatched customers were already gone.
options.why: A LEFT JOIN keeps every left-hand row. They were present after the join and removed afterwards.

options.text: The WHERE clause runs after the join, and NULL > 100 is not true.
The join condition should use WHERE instead of ON.
options.why: That would make it an inner join in effect — the same wrong result, arrived at deliberately.

options.text: Comparing NULL to a number is a syntax error.
options.why: It is legal and evaluates to unknown, which is why the row disappears silently rather than loudly.

activities.title: Grouping
activities.prompt: Given orders (customer, total) of ('a', 10), ('a', 20), ('b', 5), what does this return? One row per line, as customer|sum.
activities.explanation: GROUP BY collapses the rows into one per distinct customer, and the aggregate is computed within each group. The ORDER BY is what makes the output predictable — without it the order is unspecified, whatever your database happens to do today.
activities.code:
SELECT customer, SUM(total)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;

activities.title: Clause order
activities.prompt: Put this query into the only order the parser accepts.
activities.explanation: The written order is fixed, and it also tells you the evaluation order that matters: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after. Putting an aggregate in WHERE is an error for that reason, and putting a plain row condition in HAVING works but scans more than it needs to.

activities.title: Ranking functions
activities.prompt: Values 10, 10, 20 ordered ascending. Match each function to the ranks it produces.
activities.explanation: ROW_NUMBER never ties. RANK ties and then skips, leaving a gap. DENSE_RANK ties without skipping. Picking the wrong one produces a leaderboard that looks right until two people draw.

activities.title: Rows with no match
activities.prompt: Complete the query so it returns customers who have never ordered.
activities.explanation: This is the anti-join. Every customer survives the LEFT JOIN; the ones with no order have NULLs on the right-hand side, and IS NULL keeps exactly those. `= NULL` is legal syntax that is never true, which is why it returns nothing and looks like an empty table rather than a bug.
activities.template:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id {1};

blanks.hint: Not `= NULL`.

curricula.title: TypeScript
curricula.summary: For someone who writes JavaScript and treats the types as decoration. The course is about making the compiler carry weight rather than about annotating what you already wrote.

skills.name: Assertions, and why they are a promise

activities.title: Narrowing
activities.prompt: What does this print?
activities.explanation: Inside the `if`, TypeScript knows `value` is a string, so `.length` is allowed; after the early return it knows the only remaining possibility is number, so `.toFixed` is allowed. Neither member of the union has both methods — narrowing is what makes the union usable at all.

activities.title: Which union is usable
activities.prompt: Which of these unions can be narrowed by checking a single property?
activities.explanation: A discriminated union needs a property with a literal type that differs between members — here `ok: true` against `ok: false`. Checking the property then tells the compiler exactly which member it has. Designing unions this way is the difference between a type that helps and one you have to cast your way out of.

{ value?: string } | { error?: string }
options.why: Both members can be the empty object, so no property distinguishes them and narrowing has nothing to work with.

options.text: string[] | number[]
options.why: Both are arrays with identical properties. You can check an element, but that tells you nothing about an empty array.

options.text: Record<string, string> | Record<string, number>
options.why: Index signatures give the two members the same shape, so there is no discriminant anywhere.

activities.title: Making a missed case a compile error
activities.prompt: Complete the default branch so that adding a third shape breaks the build instead of returning undefined at runtime.
activities.explanation: In the default branch every known case has been handled, so `shape` has narrowed to `never` and the assignment is legal. Add a third member to `Shape` and it narrows to that member instead, which is not assignable to `never` — so the compiler points at this line the moment the union grows. It turns "did I update every switch?" from a memory problem into a build error.

activities.title: Utility types
activities.prompt: Given a User type with id, name and age, match each utility type to what it describes.
activities.explanation: These four cover most day-to-day type manipulation, and every one of them derives from User rather than restating it — so renaming a field updates all of them at once. Hand-written duplicates of a type are how a codebase ends up with two definitions that disagree.

activities.title: What gets inferred
activities.prompt: What is the inferred type of `mode` in `let mode = "fast";`?
activities.explanation: `let` widens a literal to its base type on the assumption that you will reassign it; `const` keeps the literal type because you cannot. This is why passing a `let` variable to a function expecting a union of string literals fails while passing the string directly works.
